top_stories.title: Berkshire Hathaway turns net buyer of stocks for first time in ~4 years under Greg Abel
points: Berkshire bought $23.5B of equities versus $3.7B sold in Q2 — its first net buying after 14 straight quarters of net selling, and the first under new CEO Greg Abel.
Cash pile fell from $397.4B to $365.5B, the steepest quarterly drawdown since 2022, though still an enormous $365B war chest.
Abel deepened the $10B Alphabet (Google's parent) private placement made in June — now worth roughly $31B, about 10% of the portfolio — a symbolic break from Buffett's historical tech aversion.
$4.5B was deployed into Berkshire's own stock (buybacks, where a company repurchases its shares to shrink share count).

Operating profit rose 16.3% to $12.98B, largely on currency gains from yen- and euro-denominated debt; net earnings doubled to $25.7B mostly on paper gains in stock holdings, not core business growth.
Closed the $6.8B acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison.

unique_angles.point: Framed the quarter primarily around the cash drop being driven by buybacks.

top_stories.title: CPI and AI earnings headline the week's market calendar
points: Stock futures were flat after major indexes capped their biggest weekly gains in months; the S&P 500 closed Friday up 0.6% at record highs after a surprise jobs report eased immediate rate-hike fears.

Wednesday's Consumer Price Index (CPI, the main gauge of consumer inflation) is expected to rise 0.2% month-on-month for both headline and core (core excludes volatile food and energy); core year-on-year seen at +2.5% vs +2.6% prior.
Thursday's Producer Price Index (PPI, inflation at the wholesale/factory level) is expected up 0.2% month-on-month, with PPI ex-food-and-energy year-on-year falling to +4.1% from +4.7%.

Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau said in-line prints would 'strengthen the case for the Fed hiking in September,' with Fed officials already split and unemployment ticking down even as the economy shed jobs.
Three AI infrastructure bellwethers report: Nebius Group (+122% year-to-date), CoreWeave (+25%) and Cerebras Systems (-35% since its May 2026 IPO) — a sharp divergence in investor reception.
Applied Materials reports Thursday; Meta launched a new open-weight AI model (model whose parameters are publicly downloadable), adding signals on AI capex confidence.

unique_angles.point: Notes these AI infrastructure names sit outside the 'Magnificent Seven' mega-cap tech group, and results will clarify the investment tier structure of the global AI build-out.
Reads flat futures as investors deliberately pausing ahead of the data.

items.title: US backs $400M scandium mine in race for rare earth sovereignty
points: The US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital signed a $400M conditional loan commitment with Australia's Sunrise Energy Metals (SREMF) for the world's first dedicated primary scandium mine.
Scandium is a rare earth element (one of 17 metals used in high-performance alloys and electronics) prized for aerospace, defense and AI-driven semiconductor manufacturing.
Production is expected in late 2028, with the US government securing first rights to output; Sunrise stock jumped 29% on the news.
Policy support includes a $218B critical mineral initiative, executive orders streamlining mine permitting and refining funding, and direct White House equity investments in miners.

Friday's Trump mining roundtable included MP Materials (MP), Century Aluminum (CENX), USA Rare Earth (USAR), Energy Fuels (UUUU), Metals Company (TMC), U.S. Antimony (UAMY) and American Resources (AREC).

Rare earths rarely occur in pure or concentrated form, so extraction is costly — leaving China dominant in processing and the sector exposed to high capex, long timelines, price swings and strict contract conditions.

items.title: Airbnb and Doximity soar on earnings and AI payback
points: Airbnb jumped 15% as revenue and bookings beat expectations; CEO Brian Chesky announced significantly higher AI spending amid strong travel demand.
Doximity surged 32% after its AI-powered search tool generated 10 times its operating cost in revenue.
Wall Street has reversed its skepticism on Big Tech AI infrastructure spending, now viewing it as justified by profit potential.

items.title: Volatility gauge drops below 15
points: The VIX (index of expected S&P 500 price swings over the next 30 days) fell to 14.90 from 20.65 a week earlier, the lowest in weeks.
Positioning implies traders expect the Fed to cut rates rather than tighten.
S&P 500 mutual funds and ETFs are up 10.6% on average year-to-date, with earnings estimate revisions hitting historic records.

items.title: Trump favors economic squeeze over strikes on Iran
points: Trump signaled he will let economic pressure build on Iran instead of launching fresh military strikes, reversing earlier bombing threats.
Iran and Oman are discussing reopening the Strait of Hormuz (key oil shipping chokepoint) to maritime traffic, but talks are unfinished.
The Pentagon's deputy urged defense contractors to boost weapons production over war-related supply concerns.
WTI crude rose 0.8% to $78.80 as traders weighed the developments.

items.title: Supreme Court approval hits record low
points: Approval of the US Supreme Court fell to record lows after an ideologically divisive term, with a majority of Americans saying justices act for political rather than legal reasons.
Trump's attacks after losing cases have accelerated the decline, notably among Republicans.
Damage also traced to hyper-partisan confirmations, polarizing rulings and ethics controversies including Justice Clarence Thomas accepting donor-funded trips.

items.title: Bond market stress and AI debt doubts
points: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is signaling an effort to keep long-term Treasury yields from spiking after rates hit a 19-year high.
Wall Street observers detect bond-market angst over debt sustainability.
Credit markets are demanding higher risk premiums on debt-financed AI data center buildouts, though short of crisis-level concern.

items.title: Taylor Farms recalls jalapeño products over salmonella
points: Taylor Farms is pulling more than a dozen prepared foods containing jalapeños, including salsas and guacamole, from major retailers.
The recall follows last month's largest-ever cyclospora outbreak (parasitic intestinal infection) tied to Mexican iceberg lettuce it supplied to chains including Taco Bell.

items.title: Wildfire forces 20,000+ evacuations in BC wine country
points: A wildfire in British Columbia's Okanagan Valley wine region has forced more than 20,000 people to evacuate, with the province declaring a state of emergency.

items.title: Hollywood confidence returns
points: Hollywood's recovery through mid-2026 has restored industry confidence in theatrical releases after years of uncertainty.

items.title: Fed independence concerns resurface
points: The White House renewed its push to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook, citing a letter 'considering' her removal under the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 opinion.

NEC Director Kevin Hassett said Fed President Kevin Warsh and the president have a 'very close, long-term relationship' and 'talk about the economy all the time' — breaking protocol that such contacts be disclosed.
Recent yield rises reflect a perceived credibility shock; bond market reaction is the key tell on whether investors still trust Fed autonomy.

items.title: Other market notes
points: Michael Burry disclosed short positions (bets a stock will fall) against Oracle and Nebius.
Retail investors are selling SpaceX shares.

issues.subject: The Race For Rare Earth Sovereignty

headlines: U.S. secures $400M funding for Australia's Sunrise Energy Metals to develop world's first primary scandium mine, with production expected in late 2028 and government priority access to output

Scandium and other rare earth elements (metals used in advanced alloys for aerospace, defense, and semiconductor industries) critical to U.S. supply chain amid China dependence and geopolitical tensions
Federal government accelerates rare earth sector support through $218B critical mineral initiative, executive orders streamlining mine permits, and direct equity investments from White House
Sunrise Energy Metals stock surged 29% on news; sector companies like MP Materials, Century Aluminum, and USA Rare Earth attending Trump's mining roundtable as policy backing intensifies
Mining sector faces persistent headwinds from high capital expenditure requirements, long execution timelines, commodity price volatility, and strict government conditions despite government backing

sections.title: The Rare Earth Push: Government Backing Drives Major Deal
points: 1. U.S. Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital signed $400M conditional loan commitment with Sunrise Energy Metals (SREMF) to develop scandium mining capability
2. Scandium is a rare earth element used in advanced alloys for aerospace, defense, and AI-driven semiconductor manufacturing—areas critical to U.S. competitiveness
3. Mine location is world's first dedicated primary scandium source; U.S. government secures first rights to production with startup expected late 2028
4. Sunrise Energy Metals stock jumped 29% on announcement, signaling investor enthusiasm for government-backed critical mineral projects

sections.title: Strategic Importance and Supply Chain Vulnerability
points: 1. China's dominance in rare earth processing creates national security concern; U.S. historically relied on Beijing for elements despite global deposits existing worldwide
2. Rare earth elements are difficult to extract profitably because they rarely occur in pure or concentrated form, creating high barriers to domestic production
3. All 17 rare earth elements have applications spanning energy infrastructure, military equipment, and semiconductor technology powering AI revolution
4. Trump administration rhetoric emphasizes 'reclaiming America's rightful place as minerals superpower' and reversing decades of outsourced mining jobs

sections.title: Mixed Outlook: Policy Support vs. Operational Challenges
points: 1. Executive orders streamline mine permitting, fast-track mineral processing/refining funding, and enable direct White House equity investments—removing historic regulatory barriers

2. Mining companies attending Friday roundtable included MP Materials (MP), Century Aluminum (CENX), USA Rare Earth (USAR), Energy Fuels (UUUU), Metals Company (TMC), U.S. Antimony (UAMY), and American Resources (AREC)
3. Sector faces persistent headwinds: heavy capital requirements, long development timelines, sharp commodity price swings, and strict government contract conditions limiting upside
4. Investor positioning divided between bullish (government backing and demand), cautious (high capex and execution risk), ETF exposure, or bearish (speculative hype concerns)

issues.subject: Morning Brief: 2 key checks on AI infrastructure and inflation

headlines: Wednesday's Consumer Price Index and Thursday's Producer Price Index reports will likely determine whether the Fed hikes rates again, with economists expecting both to rise modestly but markets focused on any surprise.

Three AI infrastructure bellwethers—Nebius Group, CoreWeave, and Cerebras Systems—report earnings this week with sharply divergent year-to-date performance (ranging from +122% to -35%), signaling uneven sentiment across the AI infrastructure sector.

White House moves to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and reported frequent communications between the president and a Fed official have reignited concerns about central bank independence at a critical moment for inflation policy.

S&P 500 closed Friday up 0.6% at record highs after a surprise jobs report eased immediate rate-hike fears, but bond market credibility concerns remain centered on whether the Fed will act decisively on pricing pressures.

Applied Materials reports Thursday and Meta launched a new open-weight AI model, providing additional signals on whether corporate confidence in AI spending and infrastructure build-out remains intact.

sections.title: Inflation Data Will Drive Fed Rate Decisions
points: 1. Wednesday's Consumer Price Index expected to rise 0.2% month-on-month (both overall and core figures excluding energy and food); core inflation year-on-year expected at +2.5% versus +2.6% previously.
2. Thursday's Producer Price Index expected to rise 0.2% month-on-month, faster than last month, with year-on-year PPI ex-food-and-energy declining to +4.1% from +4.7% previously.

3. Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau signaled that results matching expectations would 'strengthen the case for the Fed hiking in September,' despite Friday's weak jobs report creating ambiguity about rate direction.

4. Fed officials already in disagreement over next moves; unemployment ticked down even as economy shed jobs, forcing inflation prints to become the deciding factor for policy rather than labor market strength.

sections.title: Three AI Infrastructure Companies Report Amid Sector Divergence
points: 1. Nebius Group up 122% year-to-date; CoreWeave up 25%; Cerebras Systems down 35% after its May 2026 IPO—showing inconsistent investor reception despite overall AI industry bullishness.

2. These three firms occupy different landscape than 'Magnificent Seven' (mega-cap tech giants), with cloud computing firms, data center operators, and semiconductor companies showing distinct winners and losers rather than uniform gains.

3. Reports come after strong two-week table-setting with Big Tech earnings and major AI product announcements; markets at record highs, providing favorable backdrop for assessments of AI infrastructure demand.
4. Results will clarify 'who's who' in the international AI build-out and investment tier structure, with 'Magnificent Seven' performance similarly uneven this year despite sector-wide bullishness.

sections.title: Fed Independence Concerns Resurface
points: 1. White House renewed push to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook via letter citing 'considering' her removal pursuant to Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 opinion.

2. White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett stated Fed President Kevin Warsh and the president 'have a very close, long-term relationship' and 'talk about the economy all the time'—breaking with typical protocol where such conversations require press release disclosure to preserve independence.

3. Bond market reaction to these developments will be closely watched as credibility concerns already exist around Fed willingness to make 'hard decisions' on pricing pressures, with recent yield rises reflecting perceived credibility shock.

4. Independence questions emerge at critical moment when Fed faces split guidance on rate direction and inflation remains key deciding factor for policy, potentially undermining market confidence in central bank autonomy.
